items.followUp: Write three differences between Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic models.

rubric.why: This identifies the difference in the proposed electron paths.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford's unspecified electron paths with Bohr's fixed orbits.
rubric.how: Award for both sides of the contrast.

rubric.why: This identifies whether electron energies are restricted to levels.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford's non-quantized electron energies with Bohr's quantized energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for both sides of the contrast.

rubric.why: This addresses the predicted energy loss of orbiting electrons.
rubric.description: Contrasts continuous radiation in Rutherford's model with no radiation from an electron in a Bohr stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award for both sides of the contrast.

rubric.why: This compares the models' explanation of atomic stability.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford's model could not explain stability, whereas Bohr's model accounted for it.
rubric.how: Award for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: This compares the models' ability to explain atomic spectra.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford's model could not explain line spectra, whereas Bohr's model explained the hydrogen spectrum.
rubric.how: Award for the correct contrast.

modelAnswer: Rutherford's model did not specify fixed electron orbits, whereas Bohr's model has fixed orbits or energy levels.
Rutherford's model did not assign quantized energies to electrons, whereas Bohr's electrons have quantized energy levels.
In Rutherford's model, orbiting electrons would radiate energy; in Bohr's model, electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits.
Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom; Bohr's model explained atomic stability using stationary orbits.
Rutherford's model could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen; Bohr's model explained it using transitions between energy levels.

items.followUp: What is an ionic bond, and why do atoms form ionic bonds?

rubric.why: A correct definition identifies a bond as an attractive force holding particles together.
rubric.description: Defines a chemical bond as a force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together.
rubric.how: Award up to two marks for defining the bond and identifying what it holds together.

rubric.why: Atoms form bonds to reach a stable outer electronic arrangement.
rubric.description: Explains that atoms form bonds to attain a stable electronic configuration, usually an octet or duplet.
rubric.how: Award up to two marks for the stability goal and a correct reference to a filled outer shell, octet, or duplet.

rubric.why: Bond formation generally produces a more stable, lower-energy arrangement.
rubric.description: States that bonding results in a lower-energy or more stable arrangement.
rubric.how: Award the mark for this additional reason.

modelAnswer: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together.
Atoms form chemical bonds to attain a stable electronic configuration, usually a complete outer shell (octet or duplet).
Bond formation gives the atoms a more stable, lower-energy arrangement.

items.followUp: Write any four characteristics of a colloidal solution.

rubric.why: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: States that a suspension is heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award the mark for identifying its heterogeneous nature.

rubric.why: Suspended particles are comparatively large and can be seen.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles are visible to the naked eye or are comparatively large.
rubric.how: Award for either description.

rubric.why: Suspension particles settle on standing, showing that the mixture is unstable.
rubric.description: States that particles settle when the suspension is left to stand.
rubric.how: Award for describing settling on standing.

rubric.why: Suspension particles can be separated from the liquid by filtration.
rubric.description: States that a suspension can be separated by filtration.
rubric.how: Award for naming filtration or separation with a filter.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its comparatively large particles are visible to the naked eye.
The particles settle down when the suspension is left to stand.
The particles can be separated from the liquid by filtration.
